advances: This is an exact failure of monotonicity under same-mass simplex compression in continuous dimension one. Both maxima exceed the sharp $n=d=1$ target $1/4$.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
The roof is $2+4z$ on $[0,2]$ and $24-7z$ on $[2,3]$, with lower graph zero. It is concave and gives the stated original intervals. The compressed roof is half that length function, with lower graph its negative, so the centered source is convex and has the same fiber lengths. The largest is $10<21/2$.

For intervals $[l_j,u_j]$, the raw mass of the upper cap through $(k,t)$ with slope $s$ is
$$
F_{k,t}(s)=\sum_{j=0}^3\min\{u_j-l_j,\max\{0,u_j-t-s(j-k)\}\}.
$$
Its lower counterpart has mass $21-F_{k,t}(s)$ because the line has zero length in each interval. This piecewise affine function is constant in its two tails, and its only possible finite breakpoints come from equality of the threshold with an endpoint at $j\ne k$. Pure base caps must be checked separately. Any containing cap includes its parallel cap through the mark.

In either source, steep upper and lower cuts can isolate just the one-sided trace in either endpoint fiber, giving upper depth bounds $1$ and $3/2$ in raw units. At base one, steep cuts of opposite continuous orientation can both include the whole base-zero fiber and exclude the two fibers to the right. The smaller cut therefore has at most $2+6/2=5$. In the original base-two fiber, for $t\le4$ a steep lower cap $x\le t+L(z-2)$ includes all of base three and none of the bases to the left, with raw mass $3+t\le7$. For $t\ge4$ the upper cap $x\ge t+4-2z$ misses both bases to the left up to length zero and has mass $10-t+(5-t)_+\le7$. At $(2,4)$ the upper cap masses at the finite breakpoints $-4,-2,-1,1,2,4$ are respectively $9,7,7,9,12,14$ with tail masses $9,14$. Both oblique orientations have mass at least $7$, as do the pure base caps of masses $18,13$. Hence the original maximum is exactly $7/21$.

In the centered source, at $(2,0)$ with $s=-b\le0$ the formula is
$$
F_{2,0}(-b)=5+(1-2b)_++(3-b)_++\min(3,3/2+b).
$$
Its successive formulas on $[0,1/2],[1/2,3/2],[3/2,3],[3,\infty)$ are $21/2-2b$, $19/2$, $11-b$ and $8$. Reflection across $x=0$ gives $F_{2,0}(b)=21-F_{2,0}(-b)$. Thus both oblique orientations have mass at least $8$, and pure base caps still have masses $18,13$. For $t\ge0$ at base two, the cap $x\ge t-3(z-2)$ is contained in the mass-eight cap through $(2,0)$ of slope $-3$. For $t\le0$ use its reflection. The other bases have the preceding upper bounds, so the centered maximum is exactly $8/21$.

source_sections.locator: 0d7d173934db7e9e:02 A four-fiber example with no fiber carrying half the mass; (1), original and compressed calculations

statement: Let $C=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(3,0),(3,3),(2,10),(0,2)\}\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$. Its integer fibers at $0,1,2,3$ are $[0,2],[0,6],[0,10],[0,3]$. Use summed fiber length as mixed measure and divide depth by its total $21$. Every fiber has less than half the mass. The maximum normalized closed-halfspace depth over the sampled source is $7/21$ at $(2,4)$. Centering each interval at zero and keeping its length gives a convex source with the same total mass and maximum $8/21$ at $(2,0)$.
title: Centering four interval fibers increases exact mixed depth without a heavy fiber
